title: Fixture — good borderline (BM25 ranking, in brief)
text: BM25 ranking, in brief. BM25 scores a document for a query by summing per-term weights: for each query term, IDF multiplied by a saturated term-frequency factor. The saturation uses k1, usually between 1.2 and 2.0; the length-normalization parameter b defaults to 0.75, where 0 disables normalization and 1 applies it fully. IDF is computed as ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), with N the number of documents and n the number containing the term. Robertson and Walker published the formula's probabilistic basis in 1994, building on work at City University London. Because the TF factor saturates, repeating a term ten times never scores ten times higher, which is why BM25 resists keyword stuffing better than raw TF-IDF.

title: BM25 memory indexing explainer
text: Retrieval-augmented memory systems combine a fast lexical index with a slower semantic index. In a BM25 index, term frequency is saturated so repeated words stop dominating the ranking, and document length normalization keeps long journals from crowding out short precise notes. Seshat's deep store holds 14,216 chunks across genesis, library, and second-brain shelves. When a new page lands on the unified shelf, the index refresh cadence rebuilds within seconds, and a marker probe verifies the page is recallable before the write is reported as landed. Scores are recorded for every item: in the October census, 970 second-brain files contributed 10,998 chunks, and the genesis shelf contributed 424 chunks from 13 files. Quarantined material stays readable but unindexed, so noise cannot pollute recall.
